stemBlocks.value: Using a ruler, a pencil and a pair of compasses, construct accurately the square EFGH with EF = 6 cm, showing all construction lines and curves. (i) Measure and state, in centimetres, the length of the diagonal FH.
Think first: A square is just a 90° construction repeated, so the whole figure follows from one perpendicular raised at E.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p156-q12 from workbook page 156.

solutionSteps.instruction: Draw a base line and mark EF = 6 cm on it with the ruler.
Construct a perpendicular to EF at E.

contentBlocks.value: With centre E draw arcs cutting the line each side, then from those two points draw equal arcs that cross above E; join the crossing point to E

solutionSteps.instruction: Mark H on that perpendicular with EH = 6 cm.

contentBlocks.value: Compasses set to 6 cm, centre E

solutionSteps.instruction: Locate G with two arcs of radius 6 cm.

contentBlocks.value: Centre F and centre H, radius 6 cm each; they cross at G

solutionSteps.instruction: Join FG and HG to complete EFGH, then draw the diagonal FH and measure it.

strategyBlocks.value: Draw EF = 6 cm, construct a perpendicular at E, mark H 6 cm up it, then use arcs of radius 6 cm from F and H to fix G; finally join FH and measure it.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (i) FH ≈ 8.5 cm (the exact value is 6√2 = 8.49 cm)

whyThisWorks.value: Every angle of a square is a right angle and every side is equal, so a single constructed perpendicular plus two equal arcs pins the whole shape. The diagonal then closes a right-angled isosceles triangle with two sides of 6 cm, so Pythagoras gives FH = √(6² + 6²) = 6√2 — which is exactly what a correct drawing must measure.

examTip.value: Compute the expected answer with Pythagoras before you measure; if your ruler reading is more than about 0.2 cm away from it, your construction has drifted.
